newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany pinched by neighbours' truck strikes.
newsitem.headline: Germany pinched by neighbours' truck strikes.

text.p: Germany felt the pinch on Wednesday as truckers' strikes in neighbouring France and Denmark hampered deliveries of fresh produce and fish, and threatened to disrupt production at Volkswagen AG, Europe's largest carmaker.
The strike highlighted the downside of Europe's single market as French truckers blockaded highways along the border with Germany on the 10th day of their strike.
Thousands of German drivers ensnared in the blockades have been stranded for days without enough food or money.
Escalating tensions had led to fights with French truckers as some Germans tried to get around the barricades and find a way home, the German Transport Association said.
"The current situation bears witness that anarchy in the streets is threatening the power of the state. This cannot be justified by the general right to strike," the association said in a statement.
Transport Minister Matthias Wissmann appealed to his counterparts in France and Denmark to help German truck drivers stranded there, and limit the damage to German companies.
While most merchants reported prices were still steady, supplies were running short, particularly of fresh fruit from Spain and the gourmet items for which France is renowned.
German grocers and restaurateurs feared sales would drop if the strike went on.

"We got no delivery (from France) today," said chef Thomas Daehner at the restaurant La Marmite in Bonn. "The truck was stopped at the border. The poor driver can't get through and the goods are spoiling."
La Marmite buys fish, mussels and poultry from France, and will now have to find alternative supplies in Germany, he said.

The Association of German Fruit Dealers said about 1,000 produce trucks bound for Germany and the Benelux countries were stuck in France, and even more had been left unloaded because the trip was impossible.
The strike was raising German prices for citrus fruit from Spain, which arrives overland via France, the association said.

A delicatessen owner in Meckenheim said he was able to bring in his regular 70 tonne weekly shipment of fish from France by driving on back roads, but he expected sales could drop 10 to 20 percent if the strike lasted through the weekend.

The strikes have so far hit mainly gourmet fish retailers, but the situation could get worse if the Danish strike becomes more effective, said an official at the Hamburg-based Fish Industry and Wholesalers' Association.
Germany imports 19 percent of its fish from Denmark and about three percent from France, the official said.
Scandinavian salmon is being shipped in by air, boosting the price, said the owner of the Edelfisch shop in Frankfurt.
At the Kaefer and Dallmayr gourmet shops in Munich, stocks of cognac, champagne and bordeaux wines were running low, and customers had to satisfy themselves with domestic tipples.
VW union officials said the auto maker may have to cut back production at its plants in Wolfsburg and Brussels for lack of key parts that arrive from France. A decision is due on Monday.

VW imports heating and air conditioning systems for its Golf and Polo models from plants in central France and gets metal parts for the Polo from Spain. Other German car makers reported no problems with deliveries.
Employers in France agreed on Wednesday to one of the striking truckers' key demands, allowing them to retire early, but the strike went on over higher pay and shorter hours.
The Danish truckers' strike, unrelated to the one in France, has left almost a million export-bound Christmas trees rotting at the border, dealing a serious blow to the industry.
Germany takes over 60 percent of Denmark's Christmas tree exports. The Danish truckers are protesting against government plans to cut drivers' overseas subsistence allowances.
